book.title: The Telegraph All New Toughie Crossword, book 1

clue.text: Space travelling is mega-this!

indicators.note: letters that are travelling move about and arrive in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
M is the symbol for the prefix mega-, a million

explanation.surface: A gushing fan declares that space travel is the ultimate in something.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: SPACE and IS, plus M for mega, rearranged give ESCAPISM, and space travel is a mega-dose of getting away from it all.
explanation.definitionFit: Escapism is the urge to get away from everyday reality, and nothing gets further away than a trip into space.

clue.text: A second Cromwell? Not I, but definitely you!

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: not having something means it is missing, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Oliver Cromwell, Lord Protector of England
taken as written; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A playful aside: the setter disclaims being a new Cromwell but insists the reader is one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not I' removes I from OLIVER. 'You' is the person doing the puzzle, which makes the clue a wink at the reader.
explanation.definitionFit: The person reading the clue is the one working out the answers, so 'you' describes the solver.

clue.text: Warning of potential Armageddon

indicators.note: of here means made from part of what follows, so the letters lie inside those words

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A grim notice that the end of the world might be coming.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm is a signal that warns of danger, so it serves as a warning.

clue.text: Losing his head, Denis spent wildly — that's stupidity!

indicators.note: a head is the top, so losing it means the name drops its first letter
doing something wildly means doing it out of control, so these letters scatter into a new order

parts.note: the name without its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Denis lost his head and splurged his money, which was foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineptness is lack of skill or sense, a close synonym of stupidity.

clue.text: America's beginning to endanger underwater creatures

parts.note: UNRESOLVED: no clue word as captured supplies these letters; this placeholder marks the gap, perhaps a word such as Med lost from the scan
the United States of America

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The USA is starting to put marine life at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: UNRESOLVED: USA and E end the answer, but nothing in the clue as captured gives the opening MED, so this parse is incomplete and should be checked against the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: A medusa is the free-swimming jellyfish stage of a cnidarian, so medusae are creatures living underwater.

clue.text: Stylish girl's among Coventry supporters

indicators.note: to be among things is to sit in the middle of them, so one piece goes inside the other
supporters stand at either side holding something up, so only the two end letters of the word are used

parts.note: the first and last letters of the city's name
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A fashionable young woman is spotted in the crowd at a Coventry football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' looks like football fans; it is the two letters at the ends of Coventry, which hold LASS between them. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Classy is an informal adjective for elegant or high-quality, a synonym of stylish.

clue.text: Favourite's behind? — could be a throat problem

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the rump of a horse, here the one most backed to win a race
second meaning: a childhood illness with a harsh, barking cough

explanation.walkthrough: 'Favourite' sounds like a beloved pet; it is the racehorse most fancied by punters, and its hindquarters share a name with a throat illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Croup names both the hindquarters of a horse and an inflammation of the larynx and windpipe in children.

clue.text: Mad, panic leap into Trumpton vehicle?

indicators.note: something mad is crazed and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a frenzy hurls themselves into a fire engine from a children's TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: Trumpton was a 1960s British children's TV series centred on a town fire brigade. Firefighters call an engine an appliance; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire services call a fire engine an appliance, and the fire engine was the star vehicle of Trumpton.

clue.text: Penny put on endless small items, like raisins?

indicators.note: without an end, so the word loses its final letter
in a down answer, something put on another item sits beneath it, so it comes after

parts.note: sundries are small miscellaneous items, with the last letter dropped
D was the abbreviation for an old British penny

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper charges a penny for a bag of little bits such as raisins.
explanation.walkthrough: Old British pennies were written d, from the Latin denarius.
explanation.definitionFit: Raisins are grapes dried in the sun, so they are a classic sun-dried food; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Marry and divorce

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cling to them, as a spouse does in the Bible

explanation.walkthrough: The word is its own opposite: one sense means to stick fast to someone, the other to split something in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleave has two unrelated roots, one meaning to adhere closely and one meaning to separate by cutting, matching the two contrary words.

clue.text: Declining to put 50% of foreign capital into drug business

indicators.note: to put one thing into another places it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: doping is the business of giving drugs, to athletes or racehorses

indicators.note: fifty per cent means half of the named word, here its first two letters

parts.note: the first half of ROME, capital of Italy

explanation.surface: Someone is turning down a scheme to bring foreign money into the drugs trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declining to' reads as refusing, but only 'Declining' is the definition. Doping is drugging athletes or racehorses, and Rome supplies the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Drooping means sagging or flagging, the same as declining in strength or position.

clue.text: Method of teaching me Welsh hasn't altered …

indicators.note: something altered has been changed, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
W is the standard abbreviation for Welsh
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A Welsh speaker grumbles that the way they were taught has never changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the sentence on into the next clue but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: New maths was the set-theory based approach to school mathematics of the 1960s and 1970s, a teaching method.

clue.text: .. community's preference is to do without it

indicators.note: to do without something is to manage with it removed, so letters are taken away

parts.note: giving something priority is preferring it
taken as written; these are the letters removed

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue, a group declares it would rather go without something altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: The two dots at the start pick up the sentence from the clue before; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A priory is a religious house of monks or nuns, a community living under a prior or prioress.

clue.text: Early evening in old city joints is something special

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so a letter goes within the city's name

parts.note: Thebes was an ancient city of Egypt and of Greece
the first letter of evening
knees are joints of the leg

explanation.surface: A cocktail-hour gathering among old city haunts is billed as something rather special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joints' suggests bars or clubs in an evening scene; here they are body parts. E goes inside THEBES.
explanation.definitionFit: The bee's knees is an informal idiom for someone or something outstandingly good.

clue.text: Healer takes the blame — it's broken

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
to take the rap is to take the blame
the letters of it's rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor owns up to a mistake: something is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the blame' reads as one idiom, but 'takes' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A therapist treats illness or disorder of body or mind, and so is a healer.

clue.text: Following dispute, put sculptor up — in-here?

parts.note: to spar is to argue

indicators.note: in a down answer, putting a word up means writing it from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Henry Moore, the British sculptor

explanation.surface: After a row, someone is told to put their artist guest up somewhere in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' reads as giving a visitor a bed, which is what this room is for; in the wordplay 'up' just flips the sculptor's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare room is the place in a house where you put up a guest overnight.

clue.text: Holding back opposing player in Eton rugby scrum…

indicators.note: a scrum is a jumbled heap of players, so the letters are tangled into a new order

parts.note: in playground chase, the one who is 'it' plays against all the rest
taken as written
RU is the abbreviation for rugby union

explanation.surface: A forward keeps an opponent at bay in a school rugby scrum.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all sport, but the answer is a musical term. The ellipsis carries the sentence on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritenuto is an Italian performance direction meaning held back, telling players to slow down at once.

clue.text: Rich food Ali's against with declining years — her point's misplaced, though

indicators.note: the point of a girl's name is its leading letter, and misplaced says that letter is put somewhere else in the string

parts.note: taken as written
versus means against
old age is the time of life when strength declines

explanation.surface: Ali turns against fatty food as she gets older, though she may have this wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'her' is Ali, a woman's name, whose opening A moves in to sit after the S of versus. Parse partly inferred: the move is read from 'her point's misplaced'.
explanation.definitionFit: Liver sausage is a soft, fatty spread of cooked liver and pork, a notably rich food.

clue.text: .. Straightens out Scotland's peculiar problems with line-out

parts.note: unco is a Scots word for strange or unusual

indicators.note: with the line out means the letter for line is taken away

parts.note: ills are troubles or problems
L is the abbreviation for line; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone sorts out Scotland's odd troubles, rugby line-out included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line-out' looks like a rugby set piece from the clue before; it says L is taken out of ILLS.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncoil a rope or spring is to unwind it from a coil, straightening it out.

clue.text: Bumble-bee circling worried lad?

indicators.note: something worried is fretted over and pulled about, so these letters are rearranged
circling something goes all the way round it, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
the letters of lad rearranged

explanation.surface: A bumble-bee buzzes round the head of an anxious boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen glues Bumble to bee, but they split: Mr Bumble is the parish beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist, who bullies the orphan boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Bumble in Oliver Twist is a beadle, a minor parish officer, so his name stands for the office.

clue.text: Plant that's vital to spell correctly?

definitions.text: Plant that's vital to spell correctly?

parts.words: Plant that's vital to spell correctly?
parts.note: surface reading: a plant whose name is essential for good spelling
setter's reading: a magic spell, the password in the Ali Baba story that only works if this plant's name is said right

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' pretends to be about writing words correctly; it is an incantation. In Ali Baba, the robbers' cave opens only to the words 'Open Sesame'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sesame is an oil-seed plant, and its name is the key word of the magic formula that opens the cave.

clue.text: Skirt round girl widens at the waist

indicators.note: the waist is the middle of a figure, so the extra letters go into the middle of the name

parts.note: a girl's name
UNRESOLVED: the clue as captured gives no clear source for these two letters; they are what makes the name grow in the middle

explanation.surface: A skirt fitted round a girl flares out from her waist.
explanation.walkthrough: UNRESOLVED: EVE with AD in its middle gives the answer, but nothing in the clue as captured clearly supplies AD, so this parse is incomplete.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt round a problem is to avoid dealing with it directly, which is what evade means.

clue.text: Macerate ingredients for snack

indicators.note: ingredients are things mixed together, so the letters of the word are blended into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe step: soften these ingredients to make a light bite.
explanation.walkthrough: A cream tea is a British afternoon snack of tea with scones, jam and clotted cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream tea is a light afternoon meal rather than a full one, so it counts as a snack.

clue.text: It gives a boost, helping to raise Claire's ambition

indicators.note: in a down answer, raising letters means reading them from the bottom upwards
a helping is a portion, so the letters are a part of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: Something gives Claire a lift and helps her aim higher.
explanation.walkthrough: A maser is the microwave cousin of the laser; the name stands for microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
explanation.definitionFit: A maser amplifies microwave signals, so it gives them a boost.

clue.text: Dish Susan clasps one absolutely knows is for starters

indicators.note: to clasp something is to hold it tight inside, so one piece goes within the name

parts.note: Suky, or Sukey, is an old pet form of Susan, as in the nursery rhyme 'Polly put the kettle on'
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only the opening letter of each word is used

parts.note: the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A dinner guest named Susan holds forth about a dish she knows inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside SUKY, and the opening letters of the last three words follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Sukiyaki is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced beef and vegetables simmered in a pan at the table.

clue.text: Providing support for leg

definitions.note: a phrase for the answer's sense of being on someone's side

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in cricket the leg side is also called the ...

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the half of the field behind a right-handed batter's legs is the leg side, also called the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Onside can mean in agreement and supportive, and in cricket it names the leg side of the field.

clue.text: Sally regularly scours toilet

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the phrase is taken

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and so on letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A woman called Sally cleans the lavatory as part of her routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' poses as a woman's name; it is a military raid.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden charge out of a besieged position, which is exactly what a sortie is.

clue.text: Toper swallows endless stream — of liquor from here?

indicators.note: without an end, so the word loses its final letter
something swallowed ends up inside the swallower, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard, as is a toper
the river Mersey, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A drunk gulps down a stream and wonders where the drink came from.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mersey is the river of Liverpool. Somerset is a West Country county of England famous for its cider; the question mark flags the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset is the heartland of English cider making, so a drinker of its liquor could be told it comes from there.
